title: More ice had no clear link to closer peak dates across four Great Lakes in 1973-2026
abstract: We tested whether winters with more ice had closer recorded peak dates across Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. We used a fixed NOAA GLERL table for 54 winters in 1973-2026. The outcome was the mean of six absolute pairwise date gaps. The exposure was the equal-lake mean of annual maximum cover. With time and chart-era controls, the slope was -0.67 days per 10 percentage points of cover. Its conditional 95% five-year block interval was -1.59 to +0.70 days. All planned spacing checks also had intervals that included zero. Thus, the data give no clear evidence for the proposed association. This does not establish its absence. Changed chart methods, unknown peak tie rules, few winters and block-model assumptions limit inference. Raw data and annual records remain external. Code, source hashes, aggregate evidence and numerical checks support reproduction.

display.caption: Four cover-band means and regression slopes with conditional 95% block intervals. Negative slopes mean closer recorded peaks with more ice. All spacing intervals include zero.

citations.reason: The prior trend study left conditioning on ice amount open. We reuse its shared source snapshot, with new code and a four-lake outcome.
